title: Teaching AI to Find Real Vulnerabilities — Prof. David Brumley, Bugcrowd

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is measurement methodology for AI hacking capabilities. Brumley builds deterministic grading oracles, defines precision and recall metrics for vulnerabilities, introduces the audit task as an open-world grading paradigm, and explicitly warns against 'benchmaxxing security.' The V8 experiment is a benchmarking study across 41 vulnerabilities with 16 capability rungs, comparing frontier models. The core contribution is how to properly evaluate and benchmark cybersecurity AI, not how to build a single production system.

secondary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
secondary.rationale: The talk frames AI hacking as a graduated ladder of RL tasks, describes how reward signals from deterministic graders feed into RL training, and outlines next steps involving novel zero-day RL environments to push models past their current frontier. The methodology of building RL environments with clean learning signals is a post-training concern.

secondary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
secondary.rationale: The RL gym setup is an agent harness: sandboxed containers with MCP-exposed setup/read/write/grading functions, an LLM orchestrator prompted to find and exploit vulnerabilities, and a structured interaction loop. The architecture of how the model interacts with the vulnerable environment is an agent harness design.

secondary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations
secondary.rationale: MCP interfaces are used to expose grading and exploitation functions to LLMs. ExploitBench environments are distributed as Docker images with MCP interfaces. While MCP is a supporting element rather than the primary focus, it is a meaningful integration protocol in the system design.

domains.label: Security & Defense
domains.rationale: The entire talk is about offensive cybersecurity: vulnerability discovery, exploitation, sandbox escapes, and zero-day research. The speaker is Bugcrowd's chief AI and science officer and a CMU security professor. All examples (V8, Pwn2Own, DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge, AIxCC) are security-domain.

domains.label: Scientific Research
domains.rationale: The talk presents academic research methodology from a CMU professor, including controlled experiments on 41 V8 vulnerabilities, precision/recall metrics, memorization verification, and an open-science quandary about publishing weaponized exploits. The rigor and framing are research-grade.

summary: David Brumley, CMU professor and Bugcrowd's Chief AI and Science Officer, presents a methodology for teaching AI to hack at machine speed and scale, drawing an analogy to how human hackers learn through graduated difficulty. He illustrates with Richard Zhu, who went from picoCTF participant to Pwn2Own winner in two years. Brumley defines two axes for RL cybersecurity tasks—target difficulty and exploitation difficulty—and identifies critical flaws in existing benchmarks: they assume single-vulnerability programs, use LLM-as-judge (which always claims success), and cap learning by letting models repeatedly find the easiest bug. His solution is the audit task: ask models to find all vulnerabilities and submit multiple proofs, then score with precision and recall using deterministic graders that uniquify bugs via stack backtraces. On 41 V8 (Chrome's JavaScript engine) vulnerabilities, top models triggered crashes ~95% of the time, but full sandbox escape revealed sharp capability differences: Mythos achieved 73%, GPT 68%, while Gemini and Kimmy achieved 0%. Multiple CVEs showed novel, non-memorized exploitation paths, including reversing JavaScript's math.random and finding new WASM paths beyond all public work. All environments are available at exploitbench.ai as Docker images with MCP interfaces, with Mythos transcripts withheld due to NDA and weaponized exploit content.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a tightly coupled system for evaluating and training AI cybersecurity agents. Deterministic grading oracles and stack backtrace uniquification provide the trustworthy measurement infrastructure that RL training requires—without them, reward signals are corrupted by LLM-as-judge false positives and duplicate-bug counting. The audit task and capability ladder define what is measured: graduated exploitation skills from crash detection to sandbox escape, assessed via precision and recall across known and unknown vulnerabilities. MCP tool exposure and sandboxed containers are the engineering substrate enabling reproducible agent-environment interaction. The AI failure modes—reward hacking, memorization, and LLM-as-judge collapse—are precisely what the engineering design must prevent. Together, these concepts form a complete methodology: engineering constructs (oracles, containers, grading, MCP interfaces) enable clean reward signals, which enable RL training, which is then validated through memorization checks on novel zero-days. The ExploitBench benchmark operationalizes all of these into a public, reproducible evaluation framework, while the RL environment scaling represents the closing of the loop—using benchmark results to identify capability ceilings and generate fresh training data to push past them.
temporalContext: The video was published on August 1, 2026. The ExploitBench arXiv paper (2605.14153) was published May 13, 2026, and the Anthropic research page on Mythos Preview was published May 22, 2026. Bugcrowd acquired Mayhem Security on November 4, 2025, and launched RL Environments for AI model training on May 21, 2026. The DARPA AIxCC finals concluded at DEF CON 33 in August 2025, with semifinals at DEF CON 32 in August 2024. Research was conducted as of August 23, 2026. This places the talk at the leading edge of a rapidly emerging field where frontier model cybersecurity exploitation capabilities are being formally benchmarked for the first time, with both the benchmark infrastructure and the RL training pipeline having launched only months prior.
takeaways: Teaching AI to hack follows the same graduated-ladder methodology that trains human hackers like Pwn2Own winners.
Deterministic grading oracles are essential; LLM-as-judge fails in cybersecurity because LLMs always claim they succeeded.
The audit task flips the question from 'find a bug' to 'find all vulnerabilities,' enabling open-world grading with precision and recall across known and unknown bugs.
Crash triggering is not a meaningful distinguisher among models; full sandbox escape is where capability differences emerge.
On 41 V8 vulnerabilities, Mythos achieved 73% full code execution, GPT 68%, while Gemini and Kimmy achieved 0%, despite all models triggering crashes at ~50-95%.
Results are not memorized: Mythos found novel exploitation paths experts deemed impractical across multiple CVEs, including a new WASM path and reversing math.random to forge objects.
The overall V8 work was on par with a human elite researcher, producing weaponized exploits for which no public exploit existed.
All benchmark environments are freely available at exploitbench.ai as Docker images with MCP interfaces; Mythos transcripts were withheld due to NDA and non-public weaponized exploits.
Next steps use benchmarks to find where frontier models stop, then build RL environments with novel zero-day vulnerabilities to push past that frontier, at up to 10,000 environments per month.
Training cybersecurity AI is not mysterious: it requires experts building the right oracles, checking for memorization and reward hacking, and handling unknown vulnerability discovery.

concepts.name: Reinforcement learning environments for cybersecurity
concepts.explanation: RL gym setups with vulnerable programs, deterministic grading oracles, and clean reward signals for training models to discover and exploit vulnerabilities. Brumley's team generates up to 10,000 RL environments per month using a DARPA-based vulnerability mining machine.
concepts.importance: The central thesis of the talk: hacking is well-suited to RL because it has measurable oracles and graduated difficulty, and proper environment design is the key to training capable security AI.

concepts.name: LLM-as-judge failure in security
concepts.explanation: LLMs used as graders in cybersecurity always claim they successfully hacked the target, making them unsuitable for evaluation. This is a fundamental limitation that necessitates deterministic grading oracles.
concepts.importance: A critical finding that invalidates an entire class of evaluation approaches; any cybersecurity benchmark using LLM-as-judge produces unreliable results.

concepts.name: Reward hacking in multi-vulnerability programs
concepts.explanation: When models repeatedly find the easiest vulnerability in multi-bug programs to maximize reward without learning diverse exploitation skills. This stalls learning and is a direct consequence of single-vulnerability benchmark design.
concepts.importance: Identifies a specific failure mode in RL training for cybersecurity that must be addressed through audit task design and precision/recall scoring.

concepts.name: Memorization verification
concepts.explanation: Testing models against novel zero-day vulnerabilities never seen during training to confirm that successful exploits represent genuine reasoning rather than pattern memorization. Brumley provides multiple CVE examples where Mythos found novel exploitation paths experts deemed impractical.
concepts.importance: Essential for distinguishing genuine model capability from training data leakage; without memorization checks, benchmark results could be artifacts of data contamination.

concepts.name: Frontier model capability differentiation
concepts.explanation: Crash-triggering rates (~95% for top models) do not distinguish model quality, but full sandbox escape reveals sharp differences: Mythos 73%, GPT 68%, Gemini and Kimmy 0%. Only the hardest capability tier separates frontier models.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that benchmark design must target the right difficulty level; easy metrics produce misleading parity, while hard metrics reveal true capability gaps.

concepts.name: ExploitBench benchmark
concepts.explanation: A capability-graded benchmark decomposing exploitation into 16 measurable flags across 5 tiers on 41 V8 bugs, using deterministic grading oracles and MCP interfaces. Publicly available at exploitbench.ai with code on GitHub and results on HuggingFace.
concepts.importance: The primary research artifact of the talk; operationalizes the methodology into a reproducible, public evaluation framework that other researchers and model developers can use.

concepts.name: Agent harness architecture for exploitation
concepts.explanation: The system design comprising sandboxed containers with MCP-exposed tools (setup, exec, read_file, write_file, list_directory, grade) and an LLM orchestrator prompted to find AND exploit vulnerabilities. The requirement to exploit (not just find) prevents hallucination from masquerading as success.
concepts.importance: Defines how models interact with vulnerable environments; the harness architecture determines whether evaluation captures genuine exploitation capability or allows shortcuts.

concepts.name: Novel exploitation path discovery by LLMs
concepts.explanation: Evidence that top models find exploitation routes human experts deemed impractical: reversing JavaScript's math.random to forge objects (CVE-2023-670T), finding new WASM paths past all public work (CVE-2024-767965), and succeeding on x86 where internal experts doubted feasibility.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that frontier models can exhibit genuine creative reasoning in vulnerability exploitation, not just pattern matching from training data.

concepts.name: RL environment scaling with novel zero-days
concepts.explanation: Brumley's team uses a DARPA-based vulnerability mining machine to generate novel zero-day vulnerabilities for RL environments, providing up to 10,000 environments per month to partner companies to push models past their current capability frontier.
concepts.importance: Represents the practical application of the benchmarking methodology: using evaluation results to identify where models stop, then generating fresh training environments to extend that frontier.

concepts.name: Graduated difficulty ladder for AI training
concepts.explanation: The analogy between how human hackers learn (CTF problems of increasing difficulty) and how AI should be trained: through a graduated ladder of tasks across two axes—target difficulty (toy to hardened) and exploitation difficulty (find bug to crash to arb read/write to code execution).
concepts.importance: Provides the pedagogical framework for designing RL curricula; without graduated difficulty, models cannot build exploitation skills incrementally.

concepts.name: Deterministic grading oracle
concepts.explanation: A programmatic grading system that verifies exploit success through objective checks (crash detection, capability flags) rather than LLM judgment. Brumley emphasizes that LLM-as-judge always claims hacking success, making deterministic oracles essential for trustworthy evaluation.
concepts.importance: Foundation of the entire ExploitBench methodology; without deterministic grading, model capability claims in cybersecurity are unreliable.

concepts.name: Stack backtrace uniquification
concepts.explanation: Industry-standard method for distinguishing independent bugs by comparing crash stack backtraces. Used in ExploitBench to prevent duplicate vulnerability counting when models submit multiple proofs, mirroring how Microsoft and Apple crash-reporting systems uniquify bugs.
concepts.importance: Enables the audit task's precision and recall scoring by correctly identifying distinct vulnerabilities in multi-bug programs.

concepts.name: Sandboxed container environments
concepts.explanation: Reproducible, isolated containers running vulnerable applications with controlled interfaces for safe exploit testing. Each environment contains a vulnerable program, fixed binaries, and grading infrastructure.
concepts.importance: Provides the reproducible execution substrate required for fair model comparison and RL training.

concepts.name: MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool exposure
concepts.explanation: Exposing setup, exec, read_file, write_file, list_directory, and grade functions to LLM agents via MCP, enabling programmatic interaction with vulnerable targets. ExploitBench environments register MCP servers for Claude or Codex.
concepts.importance: Defines the agent-environment interaction surface; the MCP interface is how models explore, read, write, and trigger exploits in the sandboxed target.

concepts.name: Audit task methodology
concepts.explanation: An evaluation paradigm where models are asked to find ALL vulnerabilities (not just one) and submit multiple proofs. A deterministic grader uniquifies bugs via backtraces and computes precision (found/submitted) and recall (known found/total known), preventing reward hacking and enabling open-world discovery.
concepts.importance: Solves the critical flaw in existing benchmarks that assume single-vulnerability programs, enabling clean learning signals and real-world software evaluation.

concepts.name: Docker image distribution
concepts.explanation: ExploitBench environments are distributed as prebuilt Docker images available at ghcr.io/exploitbench/ and pullable from GitHub, enabling reproducible evaluation across different compute environments.
concepts.importance: Ensures benchmark reproducibility and accessibility; anyone can pull the images and test frontier models against the same V8 vulnerabilities.

concepts.name: Vulnerability chaining for sandbox escape
concepts.explanation: The process of combining multiple vulnerability primitives (e.g., addrof, fakeobj, arb_read, arb_write) to achieve full arbitrary code execution outside the V8 sandbox, representing the highest exploitation difficulty level.
concepts.importance: Sandbox escape is the meaningful capability differentiator; crash triggering alone does not distinguish model quality.

concepts.name: Single-vulnerability assumption flaw
concepts.explanation: Existing benchmarks (Cybex, CyberGym, sidebench) assume each program has exactly one vulnerability, which is rarely true in real software. This causes models to repeatedly find the easiest bug and stall their learning trajectory.
concepts.importance: Identifies a systemic design flaw in cybersecurity benchmarks that caps model learning and produces misleading capability assessments.

concepts.name: Capability ladder design
concepts.explanation: A graduated 16-flag schema across 5 tiers measuring exploitation progress from crash detection (T5) through address-of primitive, fake object, arbitrary read/write, to arbitrary code execution (T1). Each flag is deterministically graded.
concepts.importance: Provides fine-grained, graduated assessment of model exploitation capability rather than a binary pass/fail, enabling RL training with clean reward signals.

concepts.name: Open-world grading with precision and recall
concepts.explanation: A grading paradigm where models can discover unknown vulnerabilities beyond the known set, scored via precision (true vulnerabilities found / total submitted) and recall (known bugs found / total known). This prevents reward hacking and spamming while rewarding genuine novel discovery.
concepts.importance: Enables evaluation on real open-source software where the full vulnerability set is unknown, removing LLM-as-judge bias and providing cleaner learning signals.

sections.title: Two decades of teaching hacking
sections.summary: Brumley introduces himself as a CMU professor and Bugcrowd chief AI and science officer, framing the talk around designing RL environments for cybersecurity. He argues that teaching AI to hack follows the same methodology used to train human hackers.

sections.title: From CTF scoreboards to CMU
sections.summary: Story of Richard Zhu ("fluorescence"), a self-taught 17-year-old who placed second in picoCTF, was recruited to CMU, and within two years won Pwn2Own by hacking a Tesla for $375,000. His learning method—studying write-ups and practicing graduated difficulty—mirrors how Brumley trains AI models.

sections.title: A ladder of exploitation tasks
sections.summary: Defines two axes for teaching machines to hack: target difficulty (toy to hardened targets) and exploitation difficulty (finding bug to crash to arbitrary read/write to code execution). Hacking is a ladder with measurable oracles, making it well-suited to RL. Talk is divided into vulnerability discovery, weaponization, and collaboration.

sections.title: Why measuring hacking is hard and flawed grading oracles
sections.summary: Describes RL gym setup: vulnerable program in reproducible container, deterministic grading oracle (not LLM-as-judge which always claims success), MCP-exposed setup/read/write/grading functions. LLM must always be asked to exploit, not just find, to distinguish hallucination from real vulnerabilities.

sections.title: When a target has many bugs
sections.summary: Identifies a critical flaw in existing benchmarks (Cybex, CyberGym, sidebench): they assume single-vulnerability programs. Real programs have multiple bugs, and models repeatedly find only the easiest one, stalling learning. Some benchmarks give backtraces identifying the vulnerable function, further constraining exploration. Raises the catch-22 of scoring unknown vulnerabilities the model may discover.

sections.title: Deterministic graders and AIXCC scoring
sections.summary: Even DARPA's $60M Cyber Grand Challenge accidentally introduced unintended bugs in 50% of challenges, and AIxCC saw 18 unintended bugs. Brumley's solution is the audit task: ask models to find all vulnerabilities and submit multiple proofs. A deterministic grader uniquifies bugs via stack backtraces, and precision and recall balance finding unknown bugs against spamming. This open-world grading enables real open-source tasks, removes LLM-as-judge bias, and provides cleaner learning signals.

sections.title: Precision and recall for vulnerabilities
sections.summary: The audit task lets the model find and submit proofs for known and unknown vulnerabilities. Recall measures known bugs found over total known; precision measures found over submitted. This prevents reward hacking (repeatedly finding the easy bug) and spamming (submitting non-vulnerabilities). Stack backtrace uniquification distinguishes independent bugs, mirroring industry crash-reporting practice.

sections.title: Attacking V8 in Chrome
sections.summary: Brumley's team tested frontier models against V8, Chrome's JavaScript engine, which also powers Edge, Node.js, and Cloudflare Edge Workers. V8 has a sandbox where in-sandbox crashes are expected; out-of-sandbox exploitation requiring vulnerability chaining is the real target, with bounties from $10K to $100K or millions on the black market. A 16-rung capability ladder measures how far models progress from crash detection to arbitrary code execution.

sections.title: 41 vulnerabilities and a real zero day
sections.summary: On 41 verified V8 vulnerabilities (verified by Chrome security lead Sung Hin Lee), crash triggering was not a distinguisher: GPT and Mythos hit ~95% (39/41), lower models ~50%. For full arbitrary code execution, Mythos achieved 73% (30/41), GPT 68%, and Gemini and Kimmy 0%. Evidence against memorization: in CVE-2023-670T, Mythos took an exploitation route experts considered impractical, reversing JavaScript's math.random to forge objects.

sections.title: Novel exploits, ExploitBench, and next steps
sections.summary: Further evidence against memorization: CVE-2024-767965 found a new WASM path past where all public work stopped, succeeding on x86 where their own internal expert doubted feasibility; CVE-2024-0519 had no public exploit yet Mythos succeeded. The overall work was on par with a human elite researcher. All environments are available at exploitbench.ai as Docker images with MCP interfaces; Mythos transcripts were withheld due to NDA and non-public weaponized exploits, raising an open-science quandary. Next steps involve using benchmarks to find where frontier models stop, then building RL environments with novel zero-day vulnerabilities found via a DARPA-based vulnerability mining machine, providing up to 10,000 environments per month. TLDR: training cybersecurity AI is not mysterious—it requires experts building the right oracles, checking for memorization and reward hacking, and handling unknown vulnerability discovery.

organization.name: Carnegie Mellon University
organization.summary: Carnegie Mellon University is the academic institution where ExploitBench was developed. The exploitbench.ai website explicitly states 'ExploitBench is a Carnegie Mellon University project.' David Brumley is a full professor in CMU's Electrical and Computer Engineering department with a courtesy appointment in Computer Science and former director of CyLab. Co-author Seunghyun Lee is a Ph.D. student at CMU and member of the PPP and MMM hacking teams. CMU provides funding and support for ExploitBench alongside Bugcrowd.

technologies.label: ExploitBench: Capability-graded cybersecurity benchmark
technologies.summary: ExploitBench is a capability-graded benchmark for LLM cybersecurity agents developed by CMU researchers Seunghyun Lee and David Brumley. It decomposes exploitation into 16 measurable flags across 5 tiers (T5 coverage through T1 control-flow hijacking and code execution) instantiated on 41 verified V8 vulnerabilities, each carrying a $10,000 Google v8CTF bounty. The benchmark uses deterministic grading oracles (not LLM-as-judge), MCP interfaces for agent interaction, and a three-arm measurement methodology. All code and containers are open source, with public model transcripts on Hugging Face and a public leaderboard at exploitbench.ai. Epoch AI independently cataloged the benchmark, confirming 41 V8 bugs reported in 2024 or later with 16 deterministically graded flags under uniform turn budgets with multiple seeds.
technologies.role: Primary research artifact and benchmark framework; the talk's core deliverable that operationalizes the methodology into a reproducible, public evaluation framework

technologies.label: Deterministic grading oracle and audit task methodology
technologies.primary: Deterministic grading oracle for cybersecurity evaluation
technologies.summary: The deterministic grading oracle is the foundational evaluation technique that replaces LLM-as-judge in cybersecurity benchmarking. Brumley establishes that LLMs used as graders always claim hacking success, making them fundamentally unsuitable. The deterministic oracle verifies exploit success through objective programmatic checks: 16 boolean capability flags across 5 tiers, crash detection, and stack backtrace uniquification to distinguish independent bugs. The audit task methodology builds on this by asking models to find ALL vulnerabilities (not just one) and submit multiple proofs, scored via precision (true vulnerabilities found / total submitted) and recall (known bugs found / total known). This open-world grading enables evaluation on real open-source software with unknown vulnerability sets, prevents reward hacking where models repeatedly find the easiest bug, and removes LLM-as-judge bias. The approach mirrors industry crash-reporting practice (Microsoft and Apple submit backtraces and uniquify them into independent bugs).
technologies.role: Core methodology innovation presented as the solution to flawed existing benchmarks; the deterministic oracle and audit task together define how to properly evaluate and train cybersecurity AI

technologies.label: MCP-based agent harness for security evaluation
technologies.primary: MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool exposure for cybersecurity evaluation
technologies.summary: The MCP-based agent harness is the architecture that enables LLM agents to interact with sandboxed vulnerable environments through a structured tool interface. ExploitBench exposes six MCP tools (setup, exec, list_directory, read_file, write_file, grade) via interface rl.mcp.v8_exploit.v1 with a 16-flag capability bitmap. The LLM orchestrator is always prompted to exploit (not just find) vulnerabilities, preventing hallucination from masquerading as success. The harness runs in reproducible sandboxed containers with five vulnerable and four fixed prebuilt binaries, evaluated against default release builds with heap sandbox, ASLR, and stack canaries enabled. This architecture supports integration with Claude and Codex via MCP server registration, making it straightforward to test frontier models against the same V8 vulnerabilities.
technologies.role: Defines how models interact with vulnerable environments; the harness architecture determines whether evaluation captures genuine exploitation capability or allows shortcuts

technologies.label: RL environment generation pipeline for cybersecurity
technologies.primary: RL environment generation for cybersecurity training
technologies.summary: The RL environment generation pipeline is the system that closes the loop from evaluation to training. Brumley's team uses a DARPA-based vulnerability mining machine to discover novel zero-day vulnerabilities, which become the basis for new RL training environments. These environments follow a graduated difficulty ladder with two axes: target difficulty (toy problems through hardened targets like V8) and exploitation difficulty (finding a bug through crash triggering to arbitrary code execution). The pipeline provides up to 10,000 RL environments per month to partner companies including leading LLM providers. Memorization verification is built into the pipeline by testing models against novel zero-days never seen during training, with multiple CVEs showing Mythos finding exploitation paths human experts deemed impractical. The methodology mirrors how human hackers learn through CTF competitions like picoCTF, created by Brumley with approximately one million high school participants annually.
technologies.role: Next-steps vision presented at the end of the talk; uses benchmarks to find where frontier models stop, then builds RL environments with novel zero-day vulnerabilities to push past that frontier at up to 10,000 environments per month

entities.name: Anthropic Mythos Preview
entities.relation: Non-public research-preview model referenced in the talk as 'Mythos'. Achieved arbitrary code execution on 18 of 41 V8 bugs in the ExploitBench primary arm (the talk states 73%, which is 30/41 — this may reflect a different counting method or updated results). Found novel exploitation paths experts deemed impractical.

entities.name: ExploitBench V8 Hugging Face Dataset
entities.relation: Public dataset of per-cell exploitation results from the V8 benchmark with full transcripts, tool-call logs, and capability grading for public models. Referenced in the talk as the open-science artifact, with Mythos transcripts withheld due to NDA.

entities.name: Mayhem Security
entities.relation: Company founded by David Brumley, later acquired by Bugcrowd. Led the team that won DARPA's Cyber Grand Challenge and built the Mayhem automated vulnerability detection platform referenced in the talk's background.

resources.title: Bugcrowd Leadership: Dr. David Brumley, Chief AI and Science Officer
resources.why: First-party verification of the speaker's identity, dual affiliation with CMU and Bugcrowd, and key biographical claims including picoCTF creation and DARPA CGC win

resources.title: David Brumley - Electrical and Computer Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University
resources.why: First-party academic verification of the speaker's professorship, his cybersecurity research focus, and his mentorship of the PPP team relevant to the CTF competition narrative in the talk

resources.title: ExploitBench: A Capability Ladder Benchmark for LLM Cybersecurity Agents
resources.why: Directly verifies the talk's core technical claims: 41 V8 vulnerabilities, 16 capability rungs, deterministic grading oracles instead of LLM-as-judge, MCP-exposed tools (setup, exec, read_file, write_file, list_directory, grade), Mythos Preview achieving ACE on 18 of 41 bugs, GPT-5.5 reaching ACE on one bug, and the sharp capability split between public and private frontier models

resources.title: ExploitBench GitHub Repository
resources.why: Verifies the claim that all code and containers are open source. Shows the MCP interface contract (rl.mcp.v8_exploit.v1 with 16-flag capability bitmap), Docker image references at ghcr.io/exploitbench/, and links to the separate bench-v8 server and website repos

resources.title: ExploitBench - Epoch AI Benchmark Description
resources.why: Third-party verification from a respected AI benchmark registry confirming the benchmark's methodology, 41 V8 bugs all reported in 2024 or later, 16 flags grouped into 5 tiers from T5 (coverage) to T1 (control-flow hijacking and code execution), and deterministic grading approach

resources.title: AI Cyber Challenge marks pivotal inflection point for cyber defense
resources.why: First-party verification of the transcript's claim about 18 unintended bugs found during AIxCC. Also confirms the competition used real-world open-source software (Jenkins, Linux kernel, Nginx, SQLite3, Apache Tika), matching the talk's context about unintended vulnerabilities in expert-curated challenges

resources.title: DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge reveals winning models for automated vulnerability discovery and patching
resources.why: Corroborates the DARPA official page with additional detail: 18 zero-days split by language (6 C, 12 Java), 11 Java zero-days auto-patched, average cost of $152 per vulnerability found and patched, and the seven finalist teams

resources.title: DARPA AI Cyber Challenge Proves Promise of AI-Driven Cybersecurity (Semifinal 2024)
resources.why: Provides context for the AIxCC trajectory from semifinals (22 synthetic bugs) to finals (54 synthetic + 18 real bugs), supporting the transcript's narrative about the prevalence of unintended vulnerabilities even in expert-curated security challenges

resources.title: ExploitBench V8 Dataset on Hugging Face
resources.why: Verifies the claim that public model transcripts are available. Confirms the 16-capability grading schema (caps_addrof, caps_fakeobj, caps_arb_read, caps_arb_write, caps_pc_control, caps_ace, etc.) and provides the academic record for ExploitBench including failed runs and grader-gaming attempts

resources.title: Teaching AI to Find Real Vulnerabilities — David Brumley, Bugcrowd
resources.why: Independent corroboration of the talk's content, confirming the key claims: Bugcrowd Chief AI Officer identity, audit task with precision/recall, 41 V8 vulnerabilities, top models achieving 68-73% full sandbox escape, novel exploit paths, and exploitbench.ai availability

resources.title: Patterns for Building Cybersecurity Evals
resources.why: Third-party technical verification of the benchmark's structure: 41 bugs, $10K v8CTF bounty per bug, six MCP tools (setup, exec, list_directory, read_file, write_file, grade), five vulnerable and four fixed prebuilt binaries, and patch-diff prompt without reference PoC

resources.title: Wikipedia: David Brumley
resources.why: Corroborates the CMU and Bugcrowd first-party sources with additional biographical context about his academic lineage and research focus on software security

resources.title: Measuring LLMs' ability to develop exploits
resources.why: Mythos Preview is an Anthropic Claude model. ExploitBench built by CMU and Bugcrowd researchers. Mythos Preview achieves ACE on 21/41 V8 CVEs combining Baseline and Nudged variants. CVE-2023-6702 novel exploit path confirmed by co-author Seunghyun Lee.

resources.title: Bugcrowd Acquires Mayhem Security to Bring Human-Augmented AI Automation to Security Testing
resources.why: Bugcrowd acquired Mayhem Security (formerly ForAllSecure) on Nov 4, 2025. Founded 2012 by CMU researchers including David Brumley. Won DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge 2016. DEF CON Black Badge. Provides RL environments for LLM model builders.

resources.title: Bugcrowd launches Reinforcement Learning environments to help AI models learn real-world security skills
resources.why: Bugcrowd launched RL Environments for AI model training built on Mayhem Security technology, available to leading LLM providers for building security-capable AI models

resources.title: ExploitBench - Official Website and Leaderboard
resources.why: Confirms the talk's claim that environments are freely available at exploitbench.ai as Docker images with MCP interfaces. Shows the v8-bench launch, MCP server registration commands, and per-environment result pages

evidence.excerpt: this kid, just 2 years after he first learned cybersecurity, enters. And uh if you read about it at the time, he was the first one to hack a Tesla.
evidence.supports: Richard Zhu went from cybersecurity beginner to Pwn2Own winner in approximately two years

evidence.excerpt: What we found in cybersecurity is that is flawed. The LLMs will always say they were successful hacking.
evidence.supports: LLM-as-judge grading fails in cybersecurity contexts

evidence.excerpt: you won't be able to distinguish between an LLM hallucination and a real vulnerability. So, you almost always ask it to actually exploit the vulnerability.
evidence.supports: Models must demonstrate exploitation to distinguish real findings from hallucinations

evidence.excerpt: there's an assumption that the program only has one vulnerability. I don't know about you, but it's very rare to find a program for which you know there's only one vulnerability.
evidence.supports: Existing benchmarks assume single-vulnerability programs, which is unrealistic

evidence.excerpt: 50% of the hand curated challenges had unknown vulnerabilities.
evidence.supports: Even DARPA's expert-curated Cyber Grand Challenge accidentally introduced unintended bugs in half of challenges

evidence.excerpt: We look at the stack backtrace. If you've ever had your program crash on Windows or Mac, and it's like submit to Microsoft or Apple, what it's doing is it's submitting the backtrace, and they're uniquifying those into independent bugs
evidence.supports: Stack backtrace uniquification is the industry-standard method for distinguishing independent bugs

evidence.excerpt: GPT and GPT 5.5 and Mythos both achieved 95%. They were able to trigger a vulnerability 39 out of 41 times.
evidence.supports: Top models triggered V8 crashes on 39 of 41 vulnerabilities, showing crash detection is not a distinguishing metric

evidence.excerpt: Mythos was a quite surprising able to do this 73% of the time. So, 30 out of the 41 examples, Mythos was able to do this sort of full control flow hijack.
evidence.supports: Mythos achieved full arbitrary code execution on 30 of 41 V8 vulnerabilities, distinguishing it from lower models

evidence.excerpt: Mythos took a route that everyone thought would be too hard to do in practice. One of the things that Mythos was able to do was reverse JavaScript's math.random and use that to forge a
evidence.supports: Model exploitation results are not memorized; Mythos found novel exploitation paths experts deemed impractical

evidence.excerpt: CVE-2024-76 7965, it found a new WASM path past where all the public work had stop had stopped. In fact, it was unclear that there was a public exploit that worked for this.
evidence.supports: Mythos found novel WASM exploitation paths beyond all known public work, demonstrating non-memorized capability

evidence.excerpt: we knew that it we could exploit it on an arm, but actually even our internal expert didn't think that you could do it on x86 and Mythos succeeded.
evidence.supports: Mythos succeeded on x86 where internal experts doubted feasibility, further evidence against memorization

evidence.excerpt: you can just say like Claude pointed at the MCP interface and see if it can hack it.
evidence.supports: ExploitBench environments are publicly accessible with MCP interfaces for testing frontier models
